content.title: About
content.content: Winter squash (Cucurbita maxima) is a large, dense vegetable with sweet flesh. When cooked with added fat (oil or butter) it becomes tender and aromatic, commonly used in side dishes, casseroles and soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Winter squash belongs to the gourd family and is cultivated in temperate climates.
Its flesh is rich in beta‑carotene, a provitamin A compound.
Squash can be stored in a cool place for up to 6 months, making it a key winter staple.
Pumpkin seeds left after cooking are high in zinc and magnesium.
In many cultures it appears in traditional dishes such as American pumpkin pie or Russian pumpkin kasha.

items.title: High in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity and skin health.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports heart function.

items.title: Beneficial fats when cooked
items.content: A modest amount of added oil enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Low natural sugar
items.content: Winter squash has a low glycemic index, useful for blood‑sugar management.

items.title: Squash allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to squash.

items.title: High‑calorie additions
items.content: Excessive fat added during cooking raises the calorie content of the dish.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Squash contains modest oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stones in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Winter squash can be roasted, stewed, steamed or boiled. Add a drizzle of olive oil or a pat of butter at the end of cooking to boost flavor. Serve as a side, in soups, stews, or mash it into a puree.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole squash in a cool, dry, dark place at 0‑10 °C. Once cut or cooked, keep it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days.
